title: The Mirror Bench
summary: Use concave, convex and plane mirrors to land a flame on a screen, place a pin on an image and aim a spot of light.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 9.2, Reflection of light by spherical mirrors
concepts: Object inside the focus of a concave mirror
learningOutcome: The student can use the mirror equation and m = −v/u to place and size the image in concave and convex mirrors, and knows a plane mirror turned by θ turns the reflected ray by 2θ.

levels.title: Flicker’s image on the wall
levels.adds: Baseline: a concave mirror makes a real, inverted image on a screen; place the screen with 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and size the image with m = −v/u (Ex 9.1).
hints: Use the Cartesian convention: u and f are negative for a concave mirror and a real object.
1/v = 1/f − 1/u, and a negative v means the image is in front of the mirror, where a screen can catch it.
m = −v/u, and the image height is m times the flame’s height; a negative height means upside down.

levels.title: Dash in the wing mirror
levels.adds: New idea: a convex mirror has f > 0 and gives a virtual, upright, smaller image behind the mirror, found with the same equation (Ex 9.2, Example 9.4).
hints: For a convex mirror f is positive and the object still has u negative.
A positive v means the image is behind the mirror, so no screen can catch it.
m = −v/u is positive and below 1, so the image is upright and smaller.

levels.title: Zoya’s shaving mirror
levels.adds: New idea: inside the focus a concave mirror gives a virtual, upright, enlarged image; work backwards from the wanted m to the distance (Ex 9.15d, Example 9.3).
hints: For an object inside f the image is virtual and upright, so m is positive and above 1.
From the mirror equation, m = f/(f − u) with f = −F and u = −d.
Solve m = F/(F − d) for d, and check that d is smaller than F.

levels.title: Beam on the galvanometer scale
levels.adds: New idea: when a plane mirror turns by θ the reflected ray turns by 2θ, so the spot moves L tan 2θ along a wall L away (Ex 9.30).
hints: Draw the ray before and after the turn: the angle of incidence changes by θ, and so does the angle of reflection.
The reflected ray turns through twice the angle of the mirror.
The spot moves a distance L tan(2θ) on the wall; use a calculator in degrees.

misconceptions: A convex mirror can form a real image on a screen
Covering half of a mirror removes half of the image
A plane mirror turned by θ turns the reflected ray by θ
